title: Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack
why: An engineer can boot a full Oxide rack, including emulated service-processor and root-of-trust microcontrollers running real Hubris firmware, on one 32-thread mini-PC in about ten minutes, so rack-scale control-plane testing no longer needs rack-scale hardware.
notes: Voxel runs on illumos (Oxide Helios) in Rust: each sled and switch is a Propolis VM, P4 switching is handled by Oxide's SoftNPU software switch, and a 'falcon' suite wires the topology with simnet links and VNIC pairs. The author ran 6 sleds (3 networking, 3 Oxide sleds) on a Minisforum MS-A2 with a Ryzen 9 9955HX (32-thread) and 96GB RAM.

Boot uses a reusable zfs snapshot of a pre-configured sled. The Omicron control plane is installed either from source via cargo or from TUF-packaged releases (Tufaceous + the Buildomat CI tool); the shown TUF run extracted 12 zones and SP/RoT firmware from system version 23.0.0.

The real novelty is emulation, not simulation: Oxide replaced its happy-path SpSim stub with sp-emu, an open-source emulator of Cortex-M7 (STM32H753) and Cortex-M33 (LPC55) cores for illumos and Linux. Each device runs single-threaded, emulates instructions/time/interrupts, is flashed with Hubris, and speaks over a socket via MGS and IPCC.

Timing is faked by making time equal instructions: the emulator has no wall clock, so SysTick fires by counting instructions against the kernel's reload value. Hubris's non-preemptible kernel with single-priority SVCall/PendSV/SysTick/IRQs lets the emulator avoid nesting handlers.

Design rule is Bryan Cantrill's 'Prime Directive': labs run stock Oxide software with no hacks. The stated exception is sprockets PKI certs, which are generated rather than set at manufacturing and delivered by the RoT as in production; the author says this does not affect rack runtime.

Voxel is the successor to the 'a4x2' VM labs and complements physical 'racklettes' (four sleds, two switches each; four today, soon eight). All numbers and the ~10-minute figure are Oxide's own, self-reported from one engineer's setup.
summary: Voxel (Virtual OXidE Labs) is Oxide's software stack for emulating a complete rack on a single machine so its Product Assurance team can test the real Omicron control plane without scarce rack hardware. Built in Rust on illumos (Helios), it runs each sled and switch as a Propolis VM, uses the SoftNPU software P4 switch for networking, boots from reusable zfs snapshots of pre-configured sleds (built from Omicron source or TUF releases), and wires topology with the 'falcon' suite. Its key advance over the prior SpSim simulator is sp-emu, an open-source emulator of the Cortex-M7 and Cortex-M33 microcontrollers (STM32H753/LPC55) that flashes and runs actual Hubris firmware; because the emulator has no wall clock, it models time as instruction counts to drive SysTick and exceptions. The author reports spinning up 6 sleds in roughly 10 minutes on a Minisforum MS-A2 (Ryzen 9 9955HX, 96GB RAM). The project follows a 'Prime Directive' of running stock software unmodified, with a noted exception that sprockets PKI certs are generated rather than provisioned from the RoT at manufacturing. All performance and configuration figures are Oxide's self-reported claims.
novelty: full rack-scale emulation on a mini-PC via Propolis/illumos
audience: infra/platform engineers building or testing hardware control planes

title: Solving Postgres' Count Problem
why: If you run full-text search in Postgres, ParadeDB's ctid-based segment partitioning cuts COUNT visibility checks by about 95% and the single-index approach handles filtered and time-sorted queries that text-only indexes punt to separate B-trees.
notes: Visibility checking consumed over 80% of page accesses in the baseline COUNT query (1,382 of 1,707, vs 325 for postings/metadata), because every match requires fetching and decoding its ctid.

Partitioning segments by ctid (strategy derived from the Spooky LSM compaction paper) gives each segment a disjoint Postgres page range, so segments where all pages are marked all-visible skip per-row checks entirely: visibility-related page accesses dropped from 1,382 to 30.

Inverting the DocId map, from per-document ctid storage to a compressed page-number -> first-DocId-on-page column, cut buffer accesses from over 7,500 to under 400 (95%) after 1,000 row updates; works because segments are already sorted by ctid.

For terms matching more than 10% of documents, switching postings from Tantivy's BP128 (128-element bitpacked, delta-encoded blocks) to bitmaps made unions/intersections cheaper and halved p99 latency in the Wikipedia count benchmark.

Self-reported throughput (same-team Hacker News benchmark): filtered count 777 vs 78 QPS (10x), filtered Top-K BM25 820 vs 71 QPS (11.6x), Top-K by time 378 vs 17 QPS (21.7x) against TIN 1.0.4; the author states the single text column in PlanetScale's Wikipedia/StackExchange workloads hides this gap and that no single benchmark names a fastest engine.

Vendor benchmark caveats: TIN ran on a PlanetScale M-640 Intel machine, ParadeDB in an 8-CPU Docker container on an i7i.8xlarge; the authors switched from their k6 client-side benchmarker to a server-side PL/pgSQL method after seeing network latency inflate TIN's numbers (p50 3.6ms vs 1.6ms), and note bitmap/ctid optimizations require a reindex.
summary: ParadeDB's follow-up post details how it sped up COUNT and complex search queries for its Postgres full-text index, responding to PlanetScale's TIN benchmarks. Three optimizations target COUNT: ctid-based segment partitioning (from the Spooky LSM compaction paper) that lets whole all-visible segments skip visibility checks, dropping visibility page accesses from 1,382 to 30; an inverted page-to-first-DocId map that cut buffer accesses from 7,500+ to under 400 after 1,000 row updates; and bitmap postings for terms matching over 10% of documents, halving the count benchmark's p99. The author argues the deeper architectural difference is index pushdown: TIN is a text-only index that defers numeric filters and time sorts to separate B-trees, while ParadeDB (like Elasticsearch) indexes text and metadata together under one document identifier, enabling coordinated filtering and ordering. Self-reported Hacker News benchmarks show 10x to 21.7x throughput advantages on filtered and time-sorted queries, though all numbers are vendor-run on mismatched hardware. The post explicitly states no single benchmark, including its own, establishes a fastest search engine, and that the optimizations require a reindex.
novelty: segment partitioning + inverted docid map cut COUNT visibility overhead 95%
audience: Postgres/search engine implementers optimizing full-text search performance

title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, you can serve tool-using agents at roughly half the wall time and memory traffic of an all-strong-model pipeline by demoting the big model to a verifier, with success rate within one point on τ²-Bench.
notes: SpecAgent inverts the usual speculative-decoding roles: the weak model authors steps and the strong model reviews, instead of the strong model generating and checking a draft one step at a time against its own action.
The weak model drafts a segment while executing read-only tool calls (so each step is grounded in real observations) and halts before the first action that would modify the environment.

The strong model verifies the whole drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and regenerates only the first rejected step, so it decodes short verdicts plus occasional repairs rather than every step.

Self-reported results: on τ²-Bench, within one point of the strong model's success rate at roughly half the memory traffic and wall time; on AutomationBench and VitaBench, recovers 44-75% of the weak-to-strong quality gap while lowering latency and memory traffic.
In an edge-cloud setup on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens.
Abstract only: no model names, sizes, methodology for the benchmarks, or ablations are given in the provided text; all numbers are author claims.
summary: SpecAgent is a collaboration protocol for LLM tool-using agents that recasts the strong model from the author of every step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model drafts a multi-step segment while executing read-only tool calls to stay grounded in real observations, stopping before any environment-modifying action; the strong model then verifies the segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest semantically valid prefix, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification uses parallel prefill rather than autoregressive decoding, the strong model only decodes short verdicts and occasional repairs. The authors report that on τ²-Bench it lands within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the weak-to-strong quality gap while cutting latency and memory. An edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models closes 53-75% of the quality gap while the strong model emits at most half as many tokens. The provided text is the abstract only, so model identities, sizes, and benchmark methodology are not specified, and all figures are self-reported.
novelty: strong model becomes verifier of weak model's grounded tool-call drafts, not author
audience: engineers building or optimizing cost/latency of tool-using LLM agents

title: EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation
why: For agent workloads where frontier-model calls dominate the bill, routing only the hard steps to the cloud cut inference cost by up to 62% on SWE-Rebench while matching full-LLM task performance.
notes: Core finding: on long-horizon agent trajectories, only a small subset of steps needs frontier-model capability; assigning the LLM to just those steps reportedly matches running the LLM on every step.

Architecture: a small language model (SLM) runs locally as the primary solver and selectively delegates individual steps to a cloud LLM; no extra models are needed at inference time to make the routing decision.
Training: a step-level RL method jointly optimizes task-solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for each delegation decision so the SLM learns when to call the cloud.

A separate external judge-based delegation strategy is used as an analysis tool to study design choices: when to delegate, how decisions are made, what context to share, and how often to invoke the cloud LLM.
Self-reported results: cost reduction up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 while matching or beating pure-LLM execution; also deployed on a local workstation.
Caveats: numbers are authors' own; no baseline model names, cost methodology, SLM/LLM sizes, or accuracy deltas are given in the abstract text.
summary: EdgeWise is an edge-cloud framework from NVIDIA Research for running long-horizon agent tasks mostly on a local small language model (SLM), delegating only select steps to a cloud frontier LLM. The authors observe that allocating the LLM to a small subset of key steps matches full-LLM execution, so they train the SLM with a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task-solving and delegation using fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions, avoiding any additional router model at inference time. They also build an external judge-based delegation strategy to study design choices: when to delegate, how decisions are made, what context is shared with the cloud, and invocation frequency. Reported experiments show EdgeWise matching or outperforming pure-LLM execution while cutting inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with a workstation deployment showing comparable savings. All figures are self-reported in the abstract; it does not specify the SLM/LLM models used, cost accounting, or absolute accuracy.
novelty: step-level RL trains SLM to selectively delegate to cloud LLM
audience: engineers building cost-efficient long-horizon agent systems

title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
why: Diffusion LMs stall at one token per pass for lossless decoding; SPOT reports up to 3.2x throughput and 6.8x fewer target passes with a 0.62M-parameter drafter, making lossless multi-token diffusion decoding practical.
notes: The core observation: a DLM's predictions from the previous pass already hold the correct token at 92-100% of positions. What is missing is commit order, which position to fill next, not what to fill it with.

SPOT trains a 0.62M-parameter drafter that reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations; the target verifies the whole tree in one pass by checking whether each candidate equals its own next state.

For verification at nonzero temperature, SPOT uses coupled-noise (shared-Gumbel-noise) matching, which the authors say generalizes prior block-diffusion verification that assumed T=0 or a sequential proposal interface.

Reported results (self-reported, not independently verified): up to 6.8x fewer target passes and up to 3.2x throughput vs standard decoding, beating calibrated and training-free drafting baselines on every task and budget at T=0 and T=1.
The learned drafter transfers across six different DLMs without retraining per the paper. Absolute latency, hardware, model sizes, and baseline methodology are not stated in the abstract.
summary: SPOT (Speculating Positions Order Trajectory) adapts speculative decoding to diffusion language models, where standard speculative decoding fails because DLMs must choose both what token to generate and which masked position to fill. The authors note that a DLM's previous-pass predictions already supply the correct token at 92-100% of positions, so the missing signal is commit order. A 0.62M-parameter drafter reads only the target's output distributions, proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by testing whether each matches its own next state. To verify at any temperature rather than only T=0 or a sequential interface, they add coupled-noise (shared-Gumbel-noise) match verification for diffusion blocks. The paper reports up to 6.8x fewer target passes and up to 3.2x throughput versus standard decoding, wins over calibrated and training-free drafting baselines at T=0 and T=1, and transfer of the learned drafter across six DLMs. All figures are self-reported, and the abstract omits hardware, absolute latency, and baseline methodology.
novelty: speculative decoding for diffusion LMs via learned position-order prediction
audience: ML researchers/engineers optimizing diffusion language model inference

title: Unveiling The Grid: PCBs made in America, twice as fast as Shenzhen
why: High-mix, low-volume PCB assembly, the ten-of-this-hundred-of-that work that has always gone overseas, now has a US option that ships a 5-board motor controller in 4 days instead of 9 for about $165 more.
notes: The Grid is a single factory-scale robot in Massachusetts: levitating movers carry each board and its parts between solder-paste print, pick-and-place, reflow, solder, and inspection stations, with learned models, AI agents, and classic optimizers scheduling routes. Each board takes its own path, so there are no per-design changeovers and 100 different designs run as easily as 100 of one.

Named customers are described only by category: a leading EV maker, a top AI lab, and household-name tech companies, cited as proof that even large firms have high volumes of low-volume boards (test stations, tooling, R&D).

Stated roadmap: 5x capacity this year, with another large expansion in 2027; demand is said to already exceed capacity. The pitch frames fixed-line automation (SpaceX's Starlink dishes in Bastrop) as viable only at million-unit scale, positioning The Grid for everything below that.
summary: CircuitHub publicly unveiled The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that has quietly assembled printed circuit boards on demand for five years. Rather than a fixed line reconfigured per product, it uses levitating movers to route each board individually through print, place, reflow, solder, and inspection stations, scheduled by learned models, AI agents, and optimizers, eliminating per-design changeovers so mixed small-batch orders run without setup penalty. The company's own cost comparison claims a five-board, 4-layer motor controller (118 parts, 38 unique) arrives in 4 days for $630 versus roughly $465 and 9 days from a typical Shenzhen quick-turn shop once shipping and US tariffs are included. CircuitHub reports cumulative totals of 2.2M+ boards, 150M+ parts placed, and 26,000+ engineers served, and says unnamed customers include a leading EV maker and a top AI lab. It plans to 5x capacity this year with a further expansion in 2027. All figures are self-reported; the benchmark board and the Shenzhen baseline were chosen by the vendor.

title: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update
why: If you run Tailscale SSH, an already-authorized user or device can escalate past its configured local-user permissions right now, so set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 and apply the patched client the moment it ships.
notes: The flaws are mostly privilege escalation: someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may perform actions beyond their configured local user's permissions, including gaining elevated privileges.

Interim mitigation: set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restart; this kills SSH forwarding (which Tailscale says addresses several of the more serious findings) without disabling Tailscale SSH.
Patched client release targeted for end of Tuesday 27 October 2026, subject to passing tests; the page is to be updated when the build lands or the timeline slips.
Tailscale is not advising everyone to disable Tailscale SSH; it recommends reviewing SSH access policies and temporarily tightening them to only the users and devices that need access.
Exploitation is conditional on the connecting user/device permissions and system configuration; Tailscale says it is still verifying the full scope and which configurations are affected.
Investigation ran with external security specialists; four security bulletins and a blog post are referenced, with a fuller advisory and technical post promised once fixes ship.
summary: Tailscale disclosed security vulnerabilities in Tailscale SSH, most of them privilege escalation: a user or device already authorized to connect can, under certain configurations, act beyond its configured local user's permissions and potentially gain elevated privileges. Exploitability depends on the connecting user's and device's granted permissions and the system configuration, and Tailscale says it is still verifying the full scope and affected setups. The company worked with external security specialists, published four security bulletins and a blog post, and targeted a patched client release for the end of Tuesday 27 October 2026, pending successful testing. It is not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH. As interim mitigations it advises reviewing and tightening SSH access policies and setting TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled environment (then restarting) to disable SSH forwarding, which it says addresses several of the more serious findings, without turning off Tailscale SSH. A fuller advisory with confirmed vulnerabilities and affected versions, plus a technical write-up of root causes and fixes, was promised once the patch is available.
novelty: Tailscale discloses active SSH privilege-escalation vulns, pushes emergency patch
audience: engineers/ops running Tailscale SSH in production fleets

title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
why: If the paper holds, formal-math teams can drop hand-built planning and prover-orchestration pipelines: a bare agentic loop with a fast Lean 4 interface matched or beat Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus at the same model.
notes: h1 is a harness that hands a model an efficient Lean 4 interface plus verifier feedback and self-reflection, with no imposed decomposition or search structure, testing a bitter-lesson claim that scaling test-time compute beats human-designed workflows.

Authors report state-of-the-art on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, and say it settled eight previously open problems in FormalConjectures; these are self-reported results with no methodology or numeric scores given in the abstract.
At matched models, h1 is claimed to match or outperform specialized workflows Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, with pass@1 (a single attempt) often enough to solve open problems.
Ablations and matched-model comparisons against Claude Code and AxProverBase attribute cost and solve rate mainly to the efficiency of the Lean interface, not to simplicity alone.

Stated recommendation: evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing new workflows, since reported workflow gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute.
Caveat: the abstract gives no benchmark numbers, model names, compute budgets, or baseline scores, so the comparative claims cannot be verified from the text provided.
summary: h1 is a minimal agentic harness for formal theorem proving: it gives a language model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and loops on verifier feedback and self-reflection, deliberately avoiding the planning, decomposition, and prover-orchestration structures common in recent formal-math systems. The authors report state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, say it settled eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and claim that at matched models it matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, often with a single pass@1 attempt. Ablations and matched-model comparisons against Claude Code and AxProverBase indicate the efficiency of the Lean interface, rather than simplicity itself, drives cost and solve rate. The paper argues that workflow gains in prior work are often confounded with stronger models or more compute, and recommends evaluating frontier models with efficient execution feedback before designing new workflows. The abstract reports no concrete benchmark numbers, model identities, or compute budgets, so the comparative claims are self-reported and unverifiable from the provided text.
novelty: simple agentic loop beats hand-engineered theorem-proving workflows
audience: ML researchers working on formal verification and agentic reasoning

title: A story of WiFi secrets, UART lockdowns and a damaged flash memory chip
why: The OCEAN_ management Wi-Fi password on a Eufy HomeBase 2 is now derivable offline: it's HMAC-SHA256 over a device serial (predictable from a template) plus one i2c-read value, so the "secret" reduces to a single unknown field once you know the model.
notes: Target: Eufy HomeBase 2, firmware 3.4.2.2h (2026-06-05), Winbond 25Q256JWEQ (WSON8) flash. In-circuit SPI0 reads from a Raspberry Pi gave three different checksums because board power activated other components; the chip had to be desoldered and read off-board, which left a 64KB block at 0x500000 unreadable.
OCEAN_ ESSID = prefix + last 3 octets of ra0 MAC (shell script set_wifi SSID logic). The password (WPAPSK1) is set by set_wifi_pwd: if a base_param byte == 0x0C it uses z8GetSN(), else the MAC.

Credential algorithm (claimed, reversed via radare2): z8GetSN() reads 0x11 bytes over i2c command 0xC1, converts to a 32-byte string used as the HMAC-SHA256 message, with the T8010... device serial number as the key; result goes through urlsafe base64 (A-Za-z0-9-_ alphabet) and is written to NVRAM, then applied via iwpriv ra0 set WPAPSK=%s.

The only non-predictable input is z8GetSN()'s return; the serial follows a known device-type template. The author states but does not demonstrate end-to-end that this makes the password recoverable in practice.

UART lockdown: inittab runs /sbin/login.sh on askfirst, which only reaches /bin/login if NVRAM debug_log=1 or /mnt/enable_console exists; otherwise it loops. Documented debug-enable paths (a filesystem flag, or an ARP-encapsulated protocol with packets signed by a key absent from the firmware) were dead ends.

Bypass: firmware is unencrypted, so they reflashed a modified U-Boot image to drop straight to a shell. Because the main image at 0x500000 was damaged, the bootloader falls back to an intact recovery image at 0xe70000 (64-byte uImage header: magic 0x27051956, load 0x80000000, entry 0x802e04f0, payload 3,429,849 bytes, MIPS32/Linux lzma).
summary: A hardware teardown of the Eufy HomeBase 2 (firmware 3.4.2.2h) documents dumping flash from a Winbond 25Q256JWEQ chip: in-circuit SPI reads failed, forcing a desolder that damaged a 64KB block at the main image load address. Using binwalk, 7z carving, and radare2, the authors reversed the algorithm that generates the password for the OCEAN_XXXXXX management Wi-Fi. They report the password is produced by HMAC-SHA256 with the value from z8GetSN() (read over i2c, command 0xC1, 0x11 bytes) as the message and the device serial number (T8010... template) as the key, then urlsafe-base64 encoded, leaving z8GetSN() as the sole unpredictable input. UART access was blocked by an inittab-launched login.sh gated on an NVRAM debug_log flag, with no reachable way to set it; since the firmware is unencrypted, they reflashed a modified U-Boot recovery image (intact at 0xe70000) to obtain a shell. The post is informal and does not fully demonstrate practical password recovery or broader exploitation.
novelty: hardware teardown reveals Eufy HomeBase2 WiFi credential algo reversed
audience: hardware/firmware security researchers and IoT reverse engineers

title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
why: DeepSeek now sells agent-grade web search and page-to-Markdown fetch at $0.75 per 1,000 successful calls, undercutting the common web-retrieval APIs engineers wire into RAG and agent loops.
notes: Two JSON endpoints share the DeepSeek bearer key: POST /v1/tools/search (its in-house search engine, returns structured results) and POST /v1/tools/fetch (returns one page as Markdown).

Billing is per successful request, not per token or per result: $0.75 per 1,000 for each API. A call is billable only on HTTP 200 with a non-empty result; empty searches, timeouts, and other failures are not charged, and count does not change the price.

Search results carry rerank_score (0-3, >=1.5 flagged high-quality) and authority tier (0-4, -1 unknown, >=3 highly authoritative), plus snippet, a 600-800 char model-facing summary, date, and optional full content when need_content is true.
Query supports forwarded operators: site:/-site: (OR-joined for multiple), term and exact-phrase exclusion, lang:, and after:/before: date filters; query is 1-128 chars, count 1-50 (default 10).

Account-level QPS is 5 for Search and 5 for Fetch, tracked separately across API keys; Fetch adds a per-domain QPS cap. Errors use the OpenAI-compatible format; 403/404 cover security-blocked or non-extractable fetches.
Server-side tool calls made via DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex already hit these APIs and are free until per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026.
summary: DeepSeek published docs for two read-only web-retrieval APIs for agents and RAG: a Search API backed by its own search engine (POST /v1/tools/search) and a Fetch API that returns a single page as Markdown (POST /v1/tools/fetch). Both are JSON endpoints using the same bearer auth as the model API. Search accepts query operators (site:, -site:, exact-phrase and term exclusion, lang:, after:/before:) forwarded with syntax intact, and returns per-result rerank_score (0-3), authority tier (0-4), snippet, a longer model-oriented summary, date, and optional full page content via need_content. Both are billed per successful request at $0.75 per 1,000, where a call counts only on HTTP 200 with an actual result; empty searches, timeouts, and failures are free, and the count parameter does not affect price. Rate limits are 5 QPS each for Search and Fetch at the account level, with an additional per-domain cap on Fetch. Tool calls already issued server-side through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex are free until per-request billing begins November 1, 2026 (Beijing time). All figures are DeepSeek's own documentation; no independent latency or quality benchmarks are provided.
novelty: DeepSeek ships its own search/fetch API, not just a model
audience: developers building RAG/agent pipelines wanting cheap web-grounding

title: Tasfer: a text editor drawn on a 2D canvas
why: If you have ever lost a weekend to contentEditable's cross-browser quirks, this is a working MIT-licensed canvas editor engine you can drop into your own app and skip the fight.
notes: The editor paints every glyph, cursor, selection, line break, and RTL Arabic layout itself onto an HTML5 2D canvas; the browser's only role is a hidden input field that captures keystrokes and IME input (autocorrect, Arabic, Chinese) so typing works at all.
The author started with WebGL/WebGPU and hand-parsed TrueType glyph outlines to render text GPU-side, shipped little, and fell back to 2D canvas as fast and good enough.

Local-first: documents stay on-device, no sign-up, no cloud copy. Collaboration uses a self-implemented CRDT with edits sent peer-to-peer over encrypted WebRTC; a signaling server only helps peers find each other and stores nothing, and an encrypted relay is used only when a direct connection is blocked.
Scope grew beyond text to a custom canvas LaTeX renderer, syntax-highlighted code blocks, tables, and a calendar; it runs on web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android.

Two licenses: the app is AGPL (copyleft, share changes if you fork or host), the editor engine is MIT and shipped as a separate SDK package. Docs at tasfer.app/docs, code at github.com/tasferlabs/tasfer.

Solo project; the author credits Claude and other LLMs discovered over Christmas 2025 for turning 'maybe one day' features into week-long tasks. All performance and architecture claims are self-reported with no benchmarks shown.
summary: Tasfer is a text editor that abandons the browser's contentEditable API and instead renders everything itself onto an HTML5 2D canvas: letters, cursor, selection, line breaking, and right-to-left Arabic text are all measured and painted by the author's code, with a hidden input field left in place only to capture keystrokes and IME input. The author first attempted GPU rendering with WebGL/WebGPU and hand-parsed TrueType outlines before settling on 2D canvas as sufficient and fast. The result is described as local-first with no server-stored documents; collaboration runs on a self-written CRDT with peer-to-peer encrypted WebRTC sync, a stateless signaling server for discovery, and an encrypted relay only as a fallback. The project has grown to include a canvas-drawn LaTeX renderer, syntax-highlighted code blocks, tables, and a calendar, and runs on web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android. It is open source under two licenses: AGPL for the app and MIT for the editor engine, which ships as a separate SDK package. The author, working solo, credits Claude and other LLMs in late 2025 with substantially accelerating development; performance and architecture claims are self-reported.
novelty: canvas-rendered text editor bypassing contentEditable entirely
audience: devs building custom rich-text/editor components
